title: The Licence and the Shared Name
chapter: The Licence and the Shared Name
lines: The Licence and the Shared Name connects software freedom with responsibility for shared reputation.
It follows how code, services, data, and models acquired different rights and obligations.
The book then proposes separating open technical rights from participation under a protected common name.
Its central concern is reciprocity without letting a custodian become an unlimited owner.
Readers can examine this institutional proposal alongside the historical problems it tries to address.

title: Freedom to continue is uneven
lines: Software permission can preserve access to code without preserving access to reputation or customers.
The book follows that gap through the history and economics of open technology.
It also examines the different rights attached to AI data, code, models, and services.
One licence cannot perform every legal and institutional function in that environment.
This historical account prepares the proposal about the shared name.

title: Open code, reciprocal name
lines: The proposed compact keeps technical rights separate from voluntary participation under a common brand.
Using the official name would carry additional responsibilities under explicit rules.
Distinct instruments would govern the mark, contributions, economic arrangements, authority, and exit.
The custodian would have a limited mandate rather than unlimited ownership of the network's future.
These are institutional design proposals whose practicality and consequences still need testing.

title: Read the instruments separately
lines: Begin with the history before evaluating the proposed compact.
Track which instrument grants technical permission and which governs representation under the shared name.
The later chapters examine maintenance, capture, succession, and the ability to leave.
The Licence and the Shared Name offers an argument about cooperation beyond a single licence.
Read it to question how openness and responsibility might remain compatible as institutions grow.
